title: Observability stewardship: dynamic scrub rules, tiered retention, RBAC for query/trace access and operator audit trail
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Motivation:
Customers require deterministic guarantees around PII exposure, adjustable retention windows per tenant and query role, and a searchable but tamper-evident audit trail for any operator actions that touch observability streams. Current observability pipelines emit traces, logs, and metrics with coarse tenant tags and a single global retention policy; RBAC on data queries is minimal and there is no structured operator audit for ad‑hoc data pulls.

Goal:
Deliver a cohesive feature set that enables: (1) dynamic PII scrubbing rules that run at pipeline ingestion and at query time, (2) tiered retention policies configurable per tenant and signal type, (3) fine-grained RBAC for query/trace/log access that integrates with SSO groups, and (4) an append-only operator audit trail with cryptographic integrity markers and exportable evidence for compliance.

Scope out of this ticket:
- Full UI work for console rollout (handled in separate PM/Design tickets)
- On-prem packaging: limited to core APIs and policy config; packaging follow-up ticket will cover installer artifacts.

Non-goals:
- Rewriting all existing pipeline connectors; we will add a minimal adapter layer for compatibility.

Approach and trade-offs considered:
1) Scrubbing stages: ingest-time vs query-time vs hybrid. Ingest-time scrubbing yields lower risk and smaller storage costs but may remove useful context; query-time preserves raw data but increases risk of accidental exposure. Chosen approach: hybrid pipeline where tenants can opt into 'raw retention' tiers; default is ingest-time scrubbing with a per-tenant policy.
2) Rule architecture: centralized rule engine vs distributed lightweight classifiers. Centralized rule engine simplifies policy management and audit but is a single point of latency; distributed classifiers are faster but harder to sync policies. Chosen approach: policy control plane (central) + distributed enforcement agents with cached policy versioning.
3) RBAC model: role-only vs attribute-based (ABAC). ABAC needed for least privilege (roles + tenant + dataset). We'll implement role + attribute checks with clear mapping to SSO group claims to start, extendable to full ABAC later.

Major deliverables (this ticket):
- Ingest-time scrubber service with rule DSL and versioned policy store (config via Control Plane API).
- Query-time scrub hook library for read paths that enforces current policy when raw-tier data is requested.
- Retention policy engine that tags data with retention-tier metadata at write time and garbage-collection worker that respects tenant policy and legal holds.
- RBAC interceptor for observability query endpoints (traces/logs/metrics) mapping SSO group claims to access grants and logging decisions.
- Operator audit trail service: append-only event log with SHA-256 chaining, exposures logged with reason, actor, dataset, and pre/post actions; export endpoint for compliance teams.
- Integration tests covering common PII patterns, retention expiries, RBAC enforcement, and audit record generation.

Acceptance criteria (must pass before merge):
- Ingest-time scrubber correctly redacts or pseudonymizes at least 95% of test PII fixtures in CI corpus.
- Policy versioning supports rollback to a previous policy with documented migration steps.
- Retention worker deletes expired data in a test tenant while preserving legal-hold objects.
- RBAC tests prevent cross-tenant trace access; role escalation attempts produce audit entries and are rejected.
- Audit trail entries include cryptographic chain hash and are append-only (attempted mutation triggers alert in CI checks).

Implementation notes and endpoints:
- Control plane API: POST /policies/observability, GET /policies/observability/{id}, PATCH /policies/observability/{id}/activate
- Scrubber agent: runs as sidecar for pipeline workers; exposes /validate-policy-cache and /enforce (binary-compatible with existing pipeline interface).
- RBAC interceptor: middleware for /api/v1/trace/query and /api/v1/logs/search that returns 403 and logs with reason.
- Audit export: GET /audit/operators?tenant={}&from={}&to={} returns signed JSONL file.

Security considerations:
- Policy store must be encrypted at rest and key material handled via customer KMS for Private deployments.
- Audit export must be signed and integrity-checked; exports truncated by retention policy for non-admins.
- Default deny for raw-tier access; explicit allow only for SSO groups mapped to e.g., observability_read_raw.

Open questions for design/PM:
- What UX should be provided for tenants to mark datasets as 'legal hold'? (PM owning follow-up)
- How long should policy versions be retained in the control plane before archival? (default 90 days?)
- Should pseudonymization be reversible for customer support (via key escrow) or strictly one-way? (legal/compliance input required)

Links and artifacts:
- Design notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/observability/stewardship-draft
- Prototype scrubber PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/observability/pull/8942
- Threat model doc: https://drive.redwood.ai/security/obs-pii-threat-model.pdf

Stakeholders and reviewers:
- PM: Maya Patel (policy scoping)
- Security reviewer: Elena Kuznetsova
- Observability eng lead: Priya Natarajan
- Legal/compliance: Tom Reynolds

Rollout plan (phased):
Phase 1 (internal): enable ingest-time scrubber and RBAC interceptor for non-production tenants; collect metrics and false positive rates.
Phase 2 (beta): expose retention tiers and audit exports to selected customers; monitor performance impact and policy misclassification.
Phase 3 (GA): enable default policies for all hosted tenants, provide console controls and managed migration guidance.
acceptance_criteria: 95% redaction coverage on CI PII fixtures for default policy
Policy version rollback supported with documented steps
Retention worker respects legal holds and deletes expired data
RBAC prevents cross-tenant access and logs attempted violations
Audit trail entries are cryptographically chained and exportable
